documents.abstract: Construction is a high-risk industry and in Uganda it is regulated by the Occupational safety and Health Act, 2006. However, there is limited evidence on how well construction employers comply with their legal duties and why. This evidence gap has also not been reviewed. To identify, appraise and synthesize the evidence on compliance with occupational health and safety (OHS) requirements in Uganda's construction sector, the determinants of compliance and the regulatory and enforcement environment. The review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020. CORE (3 searches), Consensus and Google Scholar were searched and records imported into Zotero on 22 October 2026. A total of 226 records were identified, of which 157 unique records were screened. 8 reports out of 13 requested were assessed for eligibility. Studies were eligible if they investigated compliance, practices, injuries or regulation of OHS in Uganda's construction sector. We evaluated quality with a six-domain instrument. Results were thematically synthesized. Six studies from 2016 to 2023 were included: four cross-sectional or case studies, one regulatory review with key informant interviews and one master's thesis. Five themes emerged: the level of compliance and its measurement, organizational rather than personal determinants of compliance, outdated law and limited enforcement capacity, personal protective equipment as the most visible gap, differences between building and road sites and between firms. One study reported 95% compliance that its own scale classed as unacceptable and another reported an injury prevalence of 32.4%. No included study analyses inspection or prosecution data, or the construction-specific duties of employers under the 2006 Act. Compliance in Uganda's construction sector appears to be partial and organization-driven, with a regulatory framework described as outdated and weakly enforced. The evidence is limited, focused on Kampala and mainly cross-sectional. Five relevant reports could not be obtained. The priority areas include enforcement data, doctrinal analysis of employer duties and studies of small contractors and sites outside Kampala.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: This conclusion draws together the book’s findings on the regulation of artificial intelligence deployed by social media platforms under African human rights law. It argues that the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights remains capable of robust purposive interpretation under digital conditions, and that its foundational norms of dignity, equality, and non-domination, together with its recognition of collective as well as individual rights, offer a distinctive basis for responding to algorithmic harm. The conclusion assesses the uneven progress made across the continent, acknowledging the operationalisation of regional data protection instruments and the growth of national legislation while identifying persistent fragmentation, limited enforcement capacity, and Africa’s position as a consumer rather than a co-creator of these technologies. It ends by setting out what a rights-based digital ecosystem would require.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study explored the ethical tensions and dilemmas emerging across stakeholder groups- research administrators, faculty, and undergraduate students- regarding the use of Generative AI in academic research within faith-based higher education institutions in Mindanao, Philippines. A qualitative, holistic multiple-case study design was employed across five institutions, with fifteen participants (one administrator, one faculty member, and one student per institution) selected through purposive maximum variation sampling; semi-structured interviews were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis for within-case analysis and Merriam’s five-step approach for cross-case synthesis. Nine essential themes emerged, three per stakeholder group, reflecting dilemmas of efficiency versus authentic learning, detection versus procedural fairness, innovation versus institutional integrity, assistance versus intellectual dependency, accuracy versus fabrication, professional judgment versus consistency, convenience versus genuine learning, confidence versus guilt and fear, and reliable detection versus equitable access to support, with institutional capacity emerging as a significant mediating factor that shaped both policy formalization and enforcement consistency. In addressing a contextual gap left by secular-focused studies, this research also fills a methodological gap: prior Philippine studies on faith-based AI governance relied largely on document analysis, whereas this study uses semi-structured interviews across three stakeholder groups within each institution, capturing lived experiences of ethical decision-making. The findings provide empirical evidence of how faith-based Philippine institutions navigate Gen AI ethical dilemmas and inform institutional policy design, faculty development, reform of detection practices, and student support mechanisms, particularly in resource-limited settings where ethical governance must be adapted to available capacity.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study provides one of the first systematic examinations of Spanish-language antivaccine narratives on TikTok. Through a two-phase content analysis, we characterized antivaccine narratives on Spanish TikTok guided by the sociotechnical theory of media effects. A total of 186 vaccine posts were initially retrieved via hashtag searches conducted from Spain, with 100 antivaccine posts forming the final sample representing Spanish-language content from across Hispanic communities on TikTok. Findings indicate the dominance of conspiratorial narratives, propagated primarily by non-experts who frequently cite scientific sources to enhance credibility using TikTok features such as viral audio trends and coded lexical variations in Spanish (e.g., v4cun4, 3nf3rm3d4d, la pua, pinchazo) revealing how Spanish antivaccine narratives adapt to platform-specific features to evade detection. These narratives were linked to broader conspiracy theories, including Agenda 2030, 5 G, and the “global reset.” These results highlight persistent algorithmic blind spots for Spanish antivaccine content and underscore the need for language-specific detection and counter-messaging strategies.

Abstract Background Large language models (LLMs) achieve high scores on health-professions examinations. Whether these scores support the same interpretations as human scores remains uncertain. Spain uses parallel multiple-choice examinations for entry to specialty training in medicine (Médico Interno Residente [MIR]), nursing (Enfermero Interno Residente [EIR]), psychology (Psicólogo Interno Residente [PIR]), and pharmacy (Farmacéutico Interno Residente [FIR]). Objective Using the January 2026 MIR, EIR, PIR, and FIR examinations, this study aimed to quantify the correspondence between human and LLM item facility and to describe model accuracy, distractor selection, and performance associated with measured surface features. Methods We evaluated 839 valid items using 12 configurations: GPT-5.2 at 3 reasoning efforts and Claude Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku 4.5 (Anthropic), each under neutral and expert prompts, with one run per configuration. The primary measure was the Spearman correlation (ρ) between human and machine facility on 828 complete paired items. We examined sensitivity to panel composition, scoring, pooling, and assumed reliability; compared distractor choices with a post hoc plausibility-weighted baseline; and evaluated a surface-feature classifier. Image analyses distinguished supplied from withheld images. An exploratory LLM-judge audit assessed generated explanations. Bootstrap CIs resample items or, for distractor concordance, error events; they exclude run-to-run uncertainty. Results The highest pooled accuracy was 94.8% (795/839); all 12 configurations answered 668 of 828 paired items correctly (80.7%). Scores clustered near the ceiling among the strongest configurations. Human and machine facility correlated at 0.40 (95% CI 0.34-0.45), with estimates of 0.31 to 0.40 across panel definitions and 0.39 (95% CI 0.33-0.45) after exam-stratified pooling. The observed correlation was lower than predicted by a specified one-axis simulation with a uniform model advantage (0.63; predictive interval 0.59 to 0.66; P <.001). Among 672 model errors, dominant human-distractor selection differed from the plausibility-weighted baseline by –1.25 percentage points (95% CI –4.53 to 2.19), compatible with no difference. Surface-feature accuracy was 34.4% (289/839), similar to selecting the longest option (34.6%, 290/839). The adjusted association with model correctness was uncertain (odds ratio [OR] 0.87, 95% CI 0.72-1.04). Image-associated accuracy was lower both when images were supplied (OR 0.33, 95% CI 0.21-0.53) and when withheld (OR 0.11, 95% CI 0.08-0.16). Conclusions In this single 2026 cohort, high LLM scores coexisted with limited separation among the strongest configurations and moderate correspondence with human item difficulty. These findings caution against interpreting model scores as equivalent evidence of human competence. They do not establish clinical performance or invalidate the examinations for human candidates.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Against the backdrop of policies promoting quality enhancement and excellence in vocational education alongside educational evaluation reforms, traditional classroom teaching assessments struggle to comprehensively reflect teaching quality due to limitations such as single-dimensional data and insufficient technological empowerment. To address this, this study constructs an AI-driven multimodal data fusion model for classroom teaching evaluation. This model encompasses a five-layer technical architecture—data collection, preprocessing, feature extraction, metric calculation, and result feedback—integrating three types of multi-source heterogeneous information: teaching behavior data (based on DBSCAN clustering analysis), physiological state data (combined with ResNet-18 emotion recognition), and dynamic effect data (using TransE knowledge transfer evaluation). This enables comprehensive and precise diagnosis of the classroom teaching process. Empirical validation was conducted in smart classroom environments using S-T behavioral analysis, engagement curves, and the Rt-Ch model. Results demonstrate the model’s effectiveness in identifying critical issues such as imbalanced teaching pacing and fluctuating student engagement, significantly enhancing the comprehensiveness and objectivity of evaluations. This research not only provides a replicable technical pathway for diagnosing vocational education classroom quality but also offers theoretical support and practical examples for the deep integration of artificial intelligence and educational assessment.

Artificial intelligence (AI) tools now reach English for Specific Purposes (ESP) students through the smartphones they already carry, often before institutions have decided how these tools should be used. This qualitative case study examines how ESP students and teachers at a university in the Sultanate of Oman experienced AI-supported feedback in blended learning, and how the appeal of immediate feedback interacted with the need for learner autonomy. The data come from a wider doctoral study of mobile technology in ESP classes and comprise semi-structured interviews with ESP teachers, five focus groups with 30 second-year students from maritime, engineering and medical programmes, 81 open-ended questionnaire responses and three classroom observations. AI use was not a preset topic; it emerged from participants’ own accounts of the applications they used. Students described ChatGPT and AI speaking applications as an always-available, non-judgmental tutor that gave immediate feedback and helped them rehearse speaking, writing and professional communication with more confidence. Teachers welcomed this but worried that students might become consumers rather than producers of language. We interpret these accounts as a feedback–autonomy paradox: the support that builds confidence can also crowd out independent effort, while autonomy without guidance leaves learners unsure of their progress. Teachers managed the paradox through dialogical use of AI, recorded practice followed by peer or teacher feedback, and professionally authentic tasks, while cost, limited training and the absence of shared guidance constrained equitable access. We argue that the feedback–autonomy balance should be treated as a design decision that changes over the course of a programme, and we outline implications for ESP teachers and institutions.

This exploratory field study investigates how human-screened exam tasks generated by the large language model (LLM) GPT-4o perform in comparison with conventionally developed exam tasks with regard to selected quality criteria. Using two business administration modules at a German distance-learning university, human-screened LLM-generated tasks were integrated into submission assignments (SA) alongside instructor-created tasks. Four selected task-quality indicators were examined: objective difficulty, subjective difficulty, context relevance, and item discrimination. The analysis combines descriptive statistics with paired-sample t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, applied at three aggregation levels: SA-specific, module-level, and cross-module. The results revealed mixed and task-specific patterns. While selected indicators were numerically similar for some task pairs, statistically significant and, in one comparison, substantial differences were observed in others, particularly in objective difficulty. Given that the study examined only four task pairs that were not systematically matched and that prior human screening was conducted, the findings establish neither equivalence nor general comparability. However, the study provides initial exploratory insights from two business administration modules that can serve as a foundation for further research.

Background Scientific argumentation ability is an integrated ability in AI era. However, it’s difficult to improve learners’ scientific argumentation ability in traditional classes due to individual differences.Purpose Therefore, this study decomposed scientific argumentation ability based on the CER+R (Claim–Evidence–Reasoning–Rebuttal) fra mework and integrated these components to construct a scientific argumentation AI agent. This approach goes beyond traditional methods and makes the cultivation of scientific argumentation ability a data-driven and personalized process.Sample Participants were 18 university students enrolled in an Ecology course at a university in eastern China, with similar educational backgrounds and comparable initial performance.Design and methods A crossover experimental design was adopted, with two groups experiencing opposite sequences of AI-agent access: one used the agent first and then practiced independently, while the other practiced independently before using the agent. Guided by the ICAP and CER+R frameworks, epistemic network analysis (ENA) and lag sequential analysis (LSA) were used to examine learners’ cognition and argumentation behaviors, respectively. Descriptive and inferential statistical analyses were conducted to assess scientific argumentation performance.Results Students who practiced independently before gaining access to the AI agent demonstrated more interactive and constructive engagement. Their argumentation behaviors generally followed the CER+R framework, although rebuttals often lacked subsequent evidence or reasoning. Among the 12 students with complete test data, scientific argumentation performance improved significantly from pre-test to mid-test and post-test. Questionnaire results also showed increases in students’ trust in AI and engagement.Conclusion The findings suggest that a CER+R-based AI agent may support the development of scientific argumentation performance and positive learning attitudes. Introducing AI support after independent exploration may encourage deeper engagement, while additional scaffolding is needed to help students integrate rebuttals into complete arguments.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Introduction Craniopharyngiomas are rare sellar/suprasellar tumors with long-term postoperative morbidity, including permanent diabetes insipidus (DI) and tumor recurrence. Existing clinical tools offer limited individualized prognostication. We introduce a pilot artificial intelligence (AI) platform to hypothesize postoperative outcomes in craniopharyngioma surgery. Methods Patients with histologically confirmed craniopharyngioma who underwent surgical resection between 2008 and 2023 at a single institution were retrospectively analyzed. Clinical, radiographic, and intraoperative features (e.g., tumor dimensions, volume, intraventricular extension, surgical approach, and extent of resection) were modeled using machine learning algorithms with a unified ensemble pipeline to predict permanent DI and tumor recurrence. Explainable AI interpretation using Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) quantified individual feature-level contributions, which were integrated into a FastAPI-powered web application for interactive prediction. Results 59 patients were used in a stratified cross-validation model training, of whom permanent DI occurred in 65.5% and tumor recurrence was recorded in 28.8%. The blended Ridge-Catboost ensemble achieved the highest performance for permanent DI prediction (AUC: 0.77±0.05, F1: 0.81±0.04), and a blended Naïve Bayes-Catboost ensemble was chosen for recurrence prediction (AUC: 0.78±0.12, F1: 0.67±0.15). SHAP-based feature ranking revealed that pre-operative BMI, age, and endocrine or visual dysfunction were the strongest predictors of DI and recurrence. Surgical approach and postoperative BMI changes further modulated DI risk. The app can be accessed at tinyurl.com/craniopharyngiomas. Conclusion In this small, single-institution cohort, ensemble learning and model tuning helped stabilize model accuracy and discriminative power. This exploratory AI prototype for prognostication might eventually support data-driven risk assessment in skull base oncology.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Background The growing use of AI tools such as ChatGPT in academic settings has raised concerns about AI overtrust, yet its psychological correlates remain poorly understood. This study examined how academic self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, and extrinsic motivation are associated with AI overtrust, and tested the sequential mediating roles of performance expectancy and AI literacy in these relationships. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 300 university students in South Korea who had prior experience using AI tools for academic purposes. The questionnaire measured academic self-efficacy, intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, AI literacy, and AI overtrust. Serial mediation analysis was conducted using the PROCESS macro [1] to test direct and indirect effects, including pathways sequentially mediated by performance expectancy and AI literacy. Indirect effects were evaluated using 5,000 bootstrap samples with bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals. Results Academic self-efficacy and intrinsic motivation were both positively associated with AI overtrust: learners who reported higher confidence and greater autonomy also reported higher overtrust in AI-generated information. Extrinsic motivation was numerically more strongly associated with AI overtrust than intrinsic motivation. AI literacy was not significantly correlated with AI overtrust at the bivariate level, but showed a significant negative indirect association within the mediation model. Sequential mediation analysis further indicated that, across all three psychological traits, higher performance expectancy combined with higher AI literacy was associated with lower AI overtrust. Conclusions These findings suggest that learners with higher academic self-efficacy and stronger intrinsic motivation also tend to report higher AI overtrust. Although greater academic self-efficacy may reflect more autonomous use of AI tools, it was nonetheless associated with higher overtrust in the present sample. AI literacy education tailored to learners’ psychological profiles may help support critical thinking, ethical awareness, and responsible AI use.

With the multimedia information growing fast and fierce, intelligent systems have to be able to understand and relate information in different data modalities in a seamless manner. The current chapter is an overview of cross-modal learning and retrieval embeddings, the techniques of which are aimed at aligning text, images, audio, and video into common semantic spaces. It presents the general ideas of multimodal representation learning, such as modality-specific feature extraction, common latent space modeling and fusion strategies. The chapter discusses embedding strategies of both canonical correlation analysis and deep contrastive techniques and transformer-based multimodal networks. Important similarity measures and metric learning methods that facilitate a successful retrieval are discussed. A discussion on practical cross-modal retrieval systems, evaluation benchmarks, scalability issues, and deployment issues aims at bringing the theory into contact with the real world implementation. As well, robustness, bias and ethical responsibility are discussed. New research directions include foundation model unification and fine-grained alignment, which are used in shaping scalable and reliable multimedia intelligence systems.
topics: Advanced Image and Video Retrieval Techniques

documents.abstract: This chapter explores the evolving landscape of academic integrity in the age of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), proposing a shift from rule-based referencing towards a more relational ethos of attribution. Drawing on the postplagiarism framework, Eaton distinguishes between referencing as a technical, commodified practice and attribution as a relational, reflective act of acknowledging intellectual lineage. Eaton critiques the economic motivations behind style guide publishers and the punitive nature of citation compliance in assessment, arguing that such practices often prioritise form over substance. In contrast, attribution fosters metacognitive awareness, evaluative judgement, and communal learning. The discussion extends to the complexities introduced by GenAI, highlighting the need for ethical co-creation and responsible authorship. The chapter concludes with a call for a recalibration of assessment practices and the development of an open-access, universal citation system that supports both academic rigour and ethical engagement with knowledge.

Artificial intelligence has infiltrated the digital landscape of children at an extremely fast rate, affecting the way children learn, communicate and access information. This chapter in the book makes a case in favor of an all-encompassing curriculum in AI literacy that will help children understand how to critically analyze the systems of algorithms, defend against subtle persuasion, and identify fake media. Based on the Critical Media Literacy Theory, Persuasion Knowledge Theory, Socio-Technical Systems Theory and the Digital Resilience Frameworks, describes a modular, age-based curriculum between primary-level and secondary education. Experiential learning, gamification, and project-based assessments are some of the pedagogical strategies favored with the help of teacher training and alignment of policies. Finally, the chapter makes AI literacy a key factor to creating digitally resilient citizens who are capable of operating in algorithmically mediated spaces in a responsible, reflective and ethical manner.

Children today are growing up in digital environments where Artificial Intelligence (AI) plays a central yet often invisible role in shaping their experiences. From personalized recommendations and AI-generated academic assistance to targeted advertising and algorithmically curated content intelligent systems influence how children access information, form preferences, and make decisions. This chapter argues that AI literacy must be recognized as an essential component of contemporary school education. Drawing on an interdisciplinary review of literature in AI literacy, media studies, and education, the chapter proposes a curriculum-oriented framework based on three interconnected dimensions: operational, sociocultural and critical literacy. In response, it introduces a practical pedagogical approach centered on “questioning the machine,” encouraging students to develop habits of inquiry, reflection and ethical awareness in their interactions with AI-driven content.

Abstract Automated chest X-ray report generation reduces reporting delays in resource-constrained clinical environments. Existing vision-language models often rely on large language models or full fine-tuning. This dependence causes high computational costs and limits on-premise deployment. We propose CXRG-SVLM. This small vision-language model combines a frozen RAD-DINO medical image encoder with a 4-bit quantized Qwen2.5-3B language model adapted using 4-bit QLoRA. A multi-view fusion module integrates frontal and lateral radiographs into a compact continuous visual representation. The resulting visual tokens are projected into the language-model embedding space and concatenated with clinical-indication embeddings to form a conditioning prefix. The decoder uses its native causal self-attention over this prefix and the generated tokens to produce the Findings report. The assembled implementation reports approximately 1.99 billion loaded parameter elements, of which approximately 38.1 million are trainable, corresponding to 1.91% of this framework-reported inventory. We evaluated the model on the Indiana University Chest X-ray dataset to generate the Findings section of the radiology report. The proposed model attains a ROUGE-L score of 0.3527 and a METEOR score of 0.2744. Automated entity-level agreement varies across findings, with the strongest F1 for normal descriptors and measurable agreement for pleural effusion, pneumothorax, and mediastinal mentions under the reported rule-based evaluation. Efficiency testing shows an average generation time of 5.27 seconds per report on a single graphics processing unit. These results establish the model’s computational feasibility and motivate subsequent radiologist evaluation of factual correctness, safety, and practical usefulness. Ultimately, CXRG-SVLM demonstrates that a parameter-efficient approach with less than 2% trainable parameters maintains competitive semantic fidelity, establishing an accessible foundation for future, prospectively validated on-premise clinical decision-support tools.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This paper, developed through a literature-informed conceptual synthesis, focused on how integrating Artificial Intelligence and the Internet of Things (AIoT) enables new approaches to urban traffic management through intelligent data collection, real-time analytics, and automated decision-making. Despite rapid technological advances, existing curricula and assessment frameworks provide little guidance for competency-based assessment, learning analytics, and institutional implementation in AIoT-enhanced traffic management education. Accordingly, the authors developed conceptual frameworks that support competency-based assessment and institutional implementation for AIoT-enhanced traffic management education. Drawing on contemporary literature in AIoT, competency-based education, learning analytics, authentic assessment, and digital education, two complementary conceptual frameworks were develop. The proposed Data-Driven Assessment Competency Framework (DACF) is associated competency domains, learning outcomes, authentic assessment tasks, evidence sources, AI-assisted analytics, educator judgement, analytic rubrics, feedback, and competency decisions. The accompanying AIoT Assessment Implementation Framework (AAIF) provides direction for strategic alignment, curriculum integration, infrastructure development, educator capacity building, and continuous evaluation to support sustainable institutional implementation. The authors further present competency progression levels, worked examples of assessments, analytic rubrics, assessment weighting, human-in-the-loop assessment practices, and quality assurance processes to support transparent and evidence-informed competency assessment. Unlike existing competency, digital education, or AI literacy frameworks, DACF and AAIF integrate competency mapping, authentic assessment, learning analytics, multi-source evidence, educator judgement, and institutional implementation within a unified model tailored to AIoT-enhanced traffic management education. Finally, the paper presents policy recommendations, a structured validation roadmap, and future research priorities to guide empirical validation and advance AIoT-enhanced traffic management education for smart city mobility.

This chapter examines structured decision-making in investigative contexts, emphasising the Senior Investigating Officer’s responsibility to apply transparent, evidence-led processes, avoid cognitive pitfalls, and maintain defensible and auditable rationales under scrutiny. It contrasts fast-time and slow-time decision-making, analyses intuition, heuristics, bias, and situational awareness, and promotes deliberate analytical approaches to reduce error and improve operational effectiveness. The chapter advances an investigative mindset grounded in openness, scepticism, and structured reasoning, supported by the ABC rule, critical thinking, and systematic problem-solving models that prioritise multiple hypotheses and continuous review. It explains risk management principles, including threat, harm, and risk assessment, alongside structured frameworks such as the National Decision Model and the 5WH model to guide information-gathering and decision-making. Finally, the chapter reinforces learning through hypothesis-testing, reflective practice, and continuous review, strengthening professional judgement and supporting ethical, adaptive decision-making in complex investigations.

The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) risk assessment has enhanced analytical efficiency but raised concerns regarding transparency, accountability, and trust. This chapter examines the role of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) in improving the interpretability of AI-driven ESG analytics across the Euro-Mediterranean financial landscape. Through a systematic literature review and comparative institutional analysis, the study explores how XAI techniques support regulatory compliance, sustainable finance decision-making, and cross-border ESG risk evaluation. It also addresses challenges related to algorithmic bias, data quality, greenwashing, and accessibility, while proposing frameworks to strengthen transparent and trustworthy ESG assessment systems.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: Industry 4.0 is frequently described through its technologies: cyber-physical systems, the Internet of Things, artificial intelligence, advanced analytics, cloud and edge computing, robotics, digital twins and platform infrastructures. Such descriptions are useful, but incomplete. They explain what has become technically possible but do not adequately explain why the organisational and human consequences are so substantial. This chapter therefore defines Industry 4.0 and the wider Fourth Industrial Revolution through a socio-technical systems perspective. It distinguishes the industrial concept of Industry 4.0 from the broader societal idea of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, examines the convergence and interdependence that differentiate the present transition from earlier waves of digitisation, and considers the implications for work, knowledge, authority, identity and institutional arrangements. The central argument is that Industry 4.0 is best understood as a reconfiguration of relationships among people, technologies, organisations and institutions. Its significance lies not in the presence of intelligent technologies alone, but in the redistribution of sensing, interpretation and decision-making across human and machine actors. Human transformation is consequently not an adjunct to technological adoption. It is a constitutive element of the transformation itself.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: As flexible major selection systems, including undeclared admission, become increasingly widespread in higher education, learners' capacity for self-directed academic and career planning has become more important than ever.Although the widespread adoption of Generative AI (GenAI) has improved the efficiency of information acquisition, it also raises concerns about intensified cognitive offloading, whereby learners become overly dependent on AI-generated responses without engaging in critical thinking.To address this issue, this study proposes an AI-based integrated metacognitive scaffolding model that enables learners to use AI not merely as an information provider, but as a tool for expanding their thinking.To this end, an integrative literature review explored the theoretical relationship between metacognition and scaffolding, and a cross-mapping analysis was used to derive stage-specific design principles.In addition, a scenario-based walkthrough examined the logical applicability of the proposed model.The analysis suggests that AI-supported major exploration can be conceptually organized around the role of an Inquiring Coach.The proposed model organizes the learning process into three metacognitive phases-Planning, Monitoring, and Evaluation-and specifies stage-specific strategies, including delaying immediate answers, detecting inconsistencies and generating counter-questions, and promoting reflective self-explanation.The model also incorporates a Fading mechanism as a design principle intended to support the gradual development of learners' selfdirected exploration.This study provides conceptual design guidelines for AI-supported career education systems.It proposes a theoretical basis for shifting attention from information-delivery efficiency to designing interactions that support learners' thinking.However, the model's effects on learners' metacognition or career decision-making were not empirically tested.

Purpose The individuals with lower-limb disabilities often experience considerable difficulty during sit-to-stand (STS) transitions, limiting their independence and increasing reliance on caregivers. According to the World Health Organisation (WHO, 2023), nearly 80 million people worldwide require wheelchairs.Method This study presents the design and performance evaluation of an affordable manual sit-to-stand wheelchair that incorporates ergonomic and anthropometric design principles with a three-bar linkage mechanism, ball screw drive, scissor-lift structure, force-balancing mechanism, and optimised gear ratio to ensure stable, controlled, and energy-efficient operation without electrical actuators. Structural validation of design using finite element analysis demonstrated a maximum frame deformation of 2.2 mm and a factor of safety of 2.5 under a static load of 120 kg, confirming the mechanical reliability of the design. Human testing is conducted with 25 participants (15 wheelchair users and 10 healthy volunteers), while clinical evaluation is performed under a physiotherapist’s supervision using standardised functional assessment protocols.Result The average sit-to-stand transition time is 9.5 ± 1.8 s, with 90% of participants achieving successful independent standing. Force analysis indicated that the proposed linkage mechanism reduced the operating force to approximately 10 N, corresponding to a 45.6% reduction in user effort. Furthermore, usability assessment yielded a mean System Usability Scale (SUS) score of 86.3/100, indicating excellent user acceptance.Conclusion The findings demonstrate that the proposed STS wheelchair is a safe, mechanically robust, and cost-effective assistive mobility solution that enhances user independence, reduces caregiver burden, and improves the quality of life for individuals with mobility impairments, particularly in low-resource settings.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based non-player characters (NPCs) can support unscripted historical dialogue, but their behavior in deployed educational virtual reality (VR) settings remains underexamined. This study reports the design and field validation of a self-hosted VR platform in which a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) NPC, representing King Sejong the Great, engaged 42 international participants across 126 intercultural-learning sessions. The analytic corpus, reconstructed from retained session logs, comprised 104 sessions from 39 participants (2053 participant turns; 2053 NPC responses). Repetitive NPC response loops occurred in 33 sessions (31.7%), spanning 54 episodes and 190 responses, and co-occurred with learner-side transcript repetition in 31 of these sessions. The NPC maintained its first-person persona throughout the screened corpus, yet produced 30 biographical claims unsupported by the historical record: persona consistency did not ensure factual grounding. Prompt compliance varied by instruction type, and a post hoc implementation audit could not confirm that retrieved content contributed to individual responses. Together, these results identify persona grounding, knowledge grounding, retrieval observability, and session-level instrumentation as validation targets that deployed VR–LLM systems must address separately.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: In the current digital landscape, the success of mobile commerce is tied directly to the quality of the user interface. This study examines how shifting to a "Mobile First" philosophy fundamentally reshapes the architecture of web applications. We look beyond mere technical specifications to explore the physics of user-screen interaction—from the ergonomics of "active finger" movements to reducing page weight by stripping away bulky third-party frameworks. Our research demonstrates that leveraging native HTML5/CSS3 code alongside flexible layouts (Grid and Flexbox) creates interfaces that are not only lightning-fast but also intuitively adaptive to human behavior.

This chapter argues that defensive responses to generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and academic integrity, while understandable, focus on the wrong problem. Rather than asking how to contain or neutralise GenAI, we might ask how its emergence exposes long-standing weaknesses in assessment design and opens opportunities for transformation. Learning has always been collective and distributed across people, technologies, and contexts, yet dominant systems continue to treat knowledge as the property of isolated learners. Drawing on an entangled pedagogy perspective, the chapter challenges the individualistic assumptions underpinning traditional assessment. GenAI makes the fiction of autonomous academic work visible, exposing the fragility of product-based, grade-focused assessment. Reconceptualising academic integrity as collective, relational, and situated rather than individual and rule-based, this chapter argues for framing it not by what students must avoid but by what they must learn to do: engage ethically and purposefully with resources, including AI, while navigating complex learning contexts. Assessment is reimagined as codesigned and collaborative, with students actively shaping criteria, parameters, and outcomes. In this vision, assessment cultivates the adaptive capacity required for professional and social life, where competence emerges through collectively orchestrating human and technological resources in ways that reflect the entangled nature of learning in a complex world.

Search-and-rescue (SAR) drone swarms increasingly require multi-operator supervision, in which backup behaviors redistribute cognitive load to improve performance but introduce trade-offs in situational awareness (SA) and task engagement. Existing human-autonomy teaming interfaces present symmetric displays across all roles, ignoring the asymmetric information needs of backup providers and recipients. We developed a two-human, eight-drone Unity SAR testbed that operationalizes three team structures (independent, Operator A-busy, Operator B-busy) via event-allocation manipulation, with a SPAM (Situation Present Assessment Method)-derived in-task SA probe. Three iterative focus groups with eight human-centered design researchers and professionals yielded four display conditions: no-display baseline, effort display, urgency display, and combined. Semi-structured interviews with three SAR practitioners confirmed high realism ratings for the overall testbed and the viability of dynamic backup. A feasibility pilot study ( N = 4) revealed a significant main effect of team structure on backup count, confirming that the manipulation elicits backup behaviors as designed.

The rise of virtual reality (VR), mixed reality (MR), and augmented reality (AR) head-mounted displays (HMDs) has expanded the design space for social extended reality (XR) systems. However, creating realistic social XR experiences with high social presence remains challenging. Based on a screening of 3,414 studies and thematic analysis of 250 papers published between 2015 and 2021, followed by a validation of the resulting design space through the categorization of 258 studies published between 2022 and 2026, we identify (1) seven common social interaction patterns in AR/MR, (2) thirteen design dimensions for supporting all levels of social presence while developing social AR/MR solutions, (3) future research opportunities, and (4) a practitioner guide that translates the extracted design dimensions into actionable design considerations. Through our work, researchers, developers, and designers can develop realistic, engaging social AR/MR solutions that foster social connection and bring minds closer together.

Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) changes digital retail from consumer-led search to delegated decision making, increasing both the potential value and the agency risks of recommendation. This conceptual article asks the following: Under what architectural and governance conditions can an autonomous shopping agent earn calibrated consumer trust while supporting economically and environmentally appropriate consumption decisions? Using a purposive, multidisciplinary synthesis of signaling theory, principal–agent theory, the ability–benevolence–integrity model of trust, trustworthy AI, recommender system governance, and sustainable consumption research, we develop a process model linking four architectural features to consumer perceptions, delegation, reliance, and decision outcomes. The features are scoped provenance verification, disclosed and audited commercial incentives, faithful contrastive explanations, and active evaluation of retention, repair, refurbishment, and purchase. We argue that justified non-purchase advice can function as a credible signal of consumer alignment only when the operator is the signal sender, the advice creates observable opportunity or accountability costs, and compensation and audit arrangements make imitation more costly for a misaligned operator. The framework distinguishes perceived trustworthiness from overall trust, willingness to delegate, actual reliance, recommendation appropriateness, and lifecycle sustainability. A five-layer architecture, a worked decision example, and four testable propositions specify how missing data, conflicting preferences, uncertainty, authorization, privacy, and accountability should be handled. This article treats the applications as illustrations rather than empirical cases and concludes with limitations and an empirical research agenda focused on calibrated—not merely increased—trust.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is not new. The limitation of assessment regimes in higher education is not new. Advances in AI have raised sector-wide, urgent concerns about assessment’s limitations. Amongst all the hype, reactions, and responses—including regulators in some countries, like Australia, calling for action on assessment—I revisit the purpose of assessment evoked by David Boud, the practices of oral assessment as theorised by Gordon Joughin, and the authority of finding your student voice as conceptualised by Alison Cook-Sather. I argue that sustainable assessment in the age of AI requires oral assessment to be enacted as a learner–teacher dialogic practice infused with a student voice ethos. Rather than treating oral assessment as a technical response to AI, I position it as a relational and pedagogical practice that supports learning now while preparing students for futures in which AI will be ever-present. I situate my argument in conversation with those scholars calling for rehumanising, inclusive and socially just assessment practices.

Abstract Performing manual tasks involves ergonomic risk factors associated with musculoskeletal disorders. This paper presents an adaptive workstation designed to adjust the working height according to individual anthropometric characteristics and evaluates its effects on posture, perceived strain, and the duration of value-adding activities. The study examined abstracted manual tasks with relevance to end-of-life vehicle disassembly. A proof-of-concept study with twelve participants shows that more frequent height adjustments reduce exposure to ergonomically unfavorable joint-angle ranges and perceived strain without significantly affecting the duration of value-adding activities. Adaptive systems therefore have the potential to reduce awkward postures in end-of-life vehicle disassembly. The findings should be examined in a dedicated disassembly use case, taking into account varying product conditions and appropriate positioning of the work object for tasks requiring high force exertion. Practical Relevance : This paper presents an adaptive workstation that can be adjusted for various (dis-)assembly and maintenance applications. The findings of the proof-of-concept study suggest that adaptive systems offer prospects for reducing physical stress and strain during manual tasks.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Whole-body bone scintigraphy with Tc-99 m methylene diphosphonate (MDP) is widely used to detect osseous metastases, and artificial intelligence (AI) may support its interpretation. We developed and internally validated OsseoScan AI, a deep learning model classifying whole-body bone scans as normal or abnormal. In this retrospective single-center study at Phrapokklao Hospital, Thailand, consecutive oncologic scans from April 2021 to June 2026 were labeled using a two-tier composite reference standard. An ImageNet-21k-pretrained EfficientNetV2-B3 was trained on full-body anterior and posterior images from 5,040 scans of 4,313 patients (1,395 abnormal), partitioned at patient level into a training/validation pool (4,032 scans; 5-fold cross-validation) and a held-out test set (1,008 scans). Pooled out-of-fold AUC was 0.959 (95% CI 0.952–0.967). On the test set at the pre-specified threshold, AUC was 0.963 (0.946–0.977), sensitivity was 0.907 (0.868–0.944), specificity was 0.886 (0.862–0.910), and NPV was 0.961. Sensitivity was 1.000 for extensive, 0.925 for multifocal, and 0.725 for solitary metastases; a sensitivity-oriented threshold raised solitary-lesion sensitivity to 0.882 while flagging 40.7% of scans. Grad-CAM provided qualitative explainability. OsseoScan AI showed high discrimination in internal validation and may support worklist prioritization; external, multi-center, and prospective evaluation is required before clinical use.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Introduction: Drug use and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection remain major public health challenges, particularly among adolescents and young adults. Educational materials supported by artificial intelligence (AI) represent an innovative approach to health promotion strategies. Objective: To develop and validate an artificial intelligence-supported educational brochure for the prevention of drug use and HIV infection among adolescents and young adults. Methods: A technological development study with a mixed-methods approach was conducted at the Universidad de Ciencias Médicas de Santiago de Cuba between August and October 2026. The development of the brochure comprised three phases: literature review and scientific content curation, AI-assisted graphic design, and expert validation. Means, standard deviations, and the Content Validity Index (CVI) were calculated. Results: An educational brochure was developed in both printed and digital formats addressing the prevention of drug use and HIV infection. The overall CVI was 0.96, and mean scores ranged from 4.63 to 4.88. Overall, 93.8% of responses were rated as "Agree" or "Strongly Agree." Conclusions: The educational brochure demonstrated adequate content validity and represents a useful educational resource for strengthening the prevention of drug use and HIV infection. Artificial intelligence proved to be an effective supportive tool when its use was accompanied by expert supervision and validation.

Diabetes mellitus is a most common and chronic disease, affecting millions of people worldwide that presents substantial morbidity, mortality, and economic costs to society. This chapter helps to incorporate artificial intelligence (AI) along with metaverse for adult diabetes prediction. In this chapter, we provide an extensive review of current research and literature on AI-based diabetes prediction, concentrating specifically in machine learning (ML) methods and deep learning (DL) techniques. This report examines a wide range of datasets and preprocessing methods to help you select the right data, cleaning approaches for that data, and the algorithms best suited. Best practices in each are 200 identified and explored throughout. More studies are needed to enhance the interpretability and robustness of models for widespread clinical application. Future exploration is suggested in the creation of transparent AI inside metaverse, with particular ways to deal with personalized medicine and ethical use of patient data. Collaboration between health-care professionals, AI researchers, and virtual environment developers will be needed to take this field further forward in the realization of the full potential that metaverse has for us.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) may improve electrocardiographic detection of ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), but available studies address distinct diagnostic questions. We systematically reviewed studies evaluating AI-based STEMI detection from 12-lead electrocardiograms and separately synthesized AI performance against a clinical reference standard, AI and clinician performance against a clinical reference, and AI agreement with physician electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched from January 2010 through March 10, 2025. Bivariate random-effects models generated pooled sensitivity, specificity, and hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (AUC). Twenty-six studies comprising 539,876 ECGs were included. In 20 studies comparing AI with a clinical reference standard, pooled sensitivity was 0.95 (95% confidence interval, 0.91-0.97), specificity 0.95 (0.90-0.98), AUC 0.98 (0.97-0.99), positive likelihood ratio 19.2 (9.3-39.5), and negative likelihood ratio 0.05 (0.03-0.10). In 8 studies reporting both AI and clinician performance against a clinical reference, separate syntheses showed sensitivity of 0.91 (0.86-0.94) for AI versus 0.78 (0.69-0.85) for clinicians, specificity of 0.91 (0.82-0.96) for both, and AUCs of 0.95 and 0.90, respectively. In 7 studies using physician ECG interpretation as the comparator, AI sensitivity was 0.85 (0.70-0.94), specificity 0.99 (0.96-1.00), and AUC 0.98 (0.96-0.99). Sensitivity analyses excluding case-control designs, influential studies, and restricting analyses to deep learning models or raw waveform ECGs produced similar findings.
